partner: Vehbi Koç Foundation Sadberk Hanim Museum

ar.name: قصر الأمير بشتاك.
description:
يحتفظ قصر الأمير بشتاك ببعض أجزائه التي تدل على ما كان عليه المبنى من فخامة وجمال. ومن هذه الأجزاء، الواجهة الغربية التي تطل على شارع المعز، والواجهة الشمالية التي تطل على درب قرمز. ويقع المدخل الحالي للقصر في الواجهة الشمالية، وهو يتكون من عقد ثلاثي الفصوص. أما المدخل الأصلي للقصر فهو مسدود حالياً.  
  
ويحتفظ القصر أيضاً ببعض أجزاء من طوابقه الأول والثاني والثالث. وقد استغل المعمار موقع القصر على شارع المعز، فجعل أسفله حوانيت. ويوجد في الطابق الثاني من القصر القاعة الرئيسية التي تتكون من درقاعة يحيط بها من جهاتها الأربعة إيوانات. ويعلو الدرقاعة سقف خشبي مزخرف بوحدات هندسية جميلة، ويتدلى من أركانها الأربعة ثلاثة صفوف من المقرنصات الخشبية. كما يتوسط الدرقاعة فسقية من الرخام الملون تلطف من درجة الحرارة في القاعة. وتوجد في الطابق الثالث من القصر مجموعة من الحجرات التي كانت تمثل الحرملك حيث كانت تقيم النساء. وتطل هذه الحجرات على القاعة الرئيسية في الطابق الثاني عن طريق ما يعرف بالأغاني، وهي تتكون من شرفة ذات عقود مدببة مزخرفة تحوي بداخلها مشربيات من الخشب الخرط تتخللها شبابيك صغيرة. وتعكس تلك الأغاني حياة الترف لدى أصحاب هذا القصر. وكانت نساء القصر يجلسن خلف المشربيات لمشاهدة جلسات الطرب التي كانت تقام في الدرقاعة في الطابق الأسفل وكان يحضرها الرجال.  
  
ويلاحظ أن المواد المستخدمة في إنشاء هذا القصر روعي فيها ملاءمتها للبيئة وجو القاهرة الحار. فكانت الأحجار هي مادة البناء الرئيسية، حيث توفر عزلاً حرارياً. كذلك استخدم الرخام في الأرضيات وفي تكسية الجدران الداخلية، وزوِّدت القاعة بفسقية تتوسط الدرقاعة. كما استخدمت المشربيات التي وفرت الخصوصية وساعدت على كسر حدة ضوء الشمس وتلطيف الهواء الداخل للمبنى.

تدل الأجزاء الباقية من هذا القصر على ما كان عليه المبنى، من فخامة وجمال، يليقان بزوج ابنة السلطان الناصر محمد بن قلاوون. وقد اجتمعت فيه أروع عناصر العمارة المدنية، في مدينة القاهرة، من جدران حجرية عازلة للصوت والحرارة، وأسقف خشبية مرتفعة مزخرفة، وفسقية من الرخام الملوَّن، والمشربيات التي تكفل الخصوصية للسكان، وتخفف من حرارة وإبهار ضوء الشمس، في أشهر الصيف، والأرضيات الرخام. ونرى فيه بعض أوجه الحياة الاجتماعية، من تخصيص حجرات للنساء، تطل من خلال حجب خشبية، على قاعة الاحتفالات والاستقبالات، الخاصة بالرجال.
artist: الأمير سيف الدين بشتاك الناصري، أحد أمراء السلطان المملوكي الناصر محمد بن قلاوون وزوج إحدى بناته.  وكان معاصراً للفترة الثالثة من حكم السلطان الناصر (709 – 741 هـ / 1309 – 1340 م).
keywords: خشب خرط؛ درقاعة؛ زخرفة هندسية؛ عمارة سكنية؛ عمارة مدنية؛ قصر؛ مشربية.
partner: Ministry of Culture,Supreme Council of Antiquities

en.name: Amir Bashtak Palace.
description:
Some parts of the Amir Bashtak Palace that are still preserved stand witness as to the grandeur and beauty that the building once possessed. These parts include the western façade, which overlooks Al-Muizz Street, and the northern façade, which overlooks *Darb* (alley) Qurmuz. The present entrance to the palace is on the northern façade and is formed of a tri-lobed arch. The original entrance is at present closed.  
Portions of the first, second and third storeys of the palace are preserved. The architect took advantage of the location of the palace on Al-Muizz Street, being the main thoroughfare in medieval Cairo, and built shops below it. The main hall is located on the second floor of the palace, and consists of a central main area (*durqa'a*) surrounded on all sides by *iwan*s. The hall is characterised by a wooden ceiling decorated with exquisite geometric units. Three tiers of wooden *muqarnas* are suspended from all four corners of the hall. A polychrome marble fountain, which would ease the temperature, distinguishes the central position of the hall. The third storey of the palace consists of a series of rooms, which constituted the *harem* where the women resided. These rooms overlook the main hall on the second floor by means of what is known as *aghani*, a balcony with ornamented pointed arches, containing wooden screens (*mashrabiyyas*) of turned wood with small windows. These *aghani* reflect the life of luxury enjoyed by the owners of the palace. The women of the palace would sit behind the *mashrabiyyas* to watch the delightful gatherings of singing and music which took place in the hall on the floor below, and which were attended by the men.  
It may be observed that the materials used in the construction of this palace were adapted to the environment and the hot weather of Cairo. Stone was the principle material for building, to provide insulation from the heat. In addition, marble was used for the floors and to line the inner walls, and to further cool the hall it was provided with a fountain at the centre. Likewise, the *mashrabiyyas*, assisted in shielding the women from the sun's glare and cooling the air inside the building.

The remaining parts of this palace hint at its past grandeur and beauty, as befitted the son-in-law of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun. It included the finest elements of civil architecture in Cairo: stone walls to insulate sound and heat, decorated wooden ceilings, a polychrome marble fountain, screens to provide privacy and alleviate the heat and glare of the sun, and marble floors. Some aspects of social life are detectable, such as the allocation of special quarters for the women of the house, overlooking through wooden screens the main reception hall of the men.
artist: Amir Sayf al-Din Bashtak al-Nasiri, one of the commanders of the Mamluk sultan, al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, and the husband of one of his daughters. He was contemporary to al-Nasir Muhammad’s third reign of power (AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40).
keywords: Turned wood; Durqa'a; geometric decoration; residential architecture; civil architecture; palace; mashrabiyya.
partner: Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Supreme Council of Antiquities

es.name: Palacio del Emir Bashtak.
description:
Lo que queda del palacio del Emir Bashtak deja patente la grandeza y la hermosura que el edificio tuvo en su momento. Entre las partes que se conservan están la fachada occidental, que domina la calle al-Muizz, y la fachada norte, que da al *darb* ('callejón') de Qurmuz. La actual entrada a palacio se ubica en la fachada norte y está formada por un arco trilobulado; la entrada original está cerrada.  
Se conservan partes de los pisos primero, segundo y tercero del palacio. El arquitecto, aprovechando la circunstancia de que el palacio estaba en esta calle, la vía más importante en El Cairo medieval, construyó tiendas en la parte inferior. La sala principal está en la segunda planta y consta de un área central principal *(durqaa)* rodeada de *iwan*. Esta sala se caracteriza por su techumbre de madera con sofisticados motivos geométricos. De los cuatro ángulos cuelgan tres filas de mocárabes también de madera. En el centro hay una fuente de mármol polícromo que servía para suavizar la temperatura. El tercer piso está formado por una serie de habitaciones que formaban el harén o zona de las mujeres. Estas habitaciones dan a la sala principal del segundo piso a través de un *agani*, balcones con vanos de arco apuntado y celosías de madera *(mashrabiyya)* con pequeñas ventanas. Estos *agani* son reflejo del lujo del que disfrutaban los dueños del palacio. Las mujeres de palacio se sentaban tras la *mashrabiyya* para contemplar las agradables reuniones, amenizadas por cantantes y músicos, que se celebraban en la sala del piso inferior, a las que sólo asistían los hombres.  
Cabe destacar que los materiales que se usaron en la construcción de este palacio se adaptaron al entorno y al clima caluroso de El Cairo. Se usó, sobre todo, piedra para aislar del calor, así como mármol para los suelos y para revestir las paredes interiores; la sala se refrescaba aún más gracias a la fuente central. De igual modo, las *mashrabiyya* protegían a las mujeres del resplandor del sol pero dejaban pasar el aire para refrescar el interior.

Los restos de este palacio hablan de un pasado de lujo y belleza, como correspondía al yerno del sultán al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun. Reúne los mejores elementos de la arquitectura civil de El Cairo: muros de piedra para aislar del ruido y el calor, exquisitos techos de madera, una fuente de mármol de colores, *mashrabiyya* para aportar intimidad y proteger del calor y la luz del sol en verano, y suelos de mármol. El palacio refleja aspectos de la vida social, como la asignación de habitaciones especiales para las mujeres que dominan, a través de celosías, la sala de recepciones de los hombres.
artist: Emir Sayf al-Din Bashtak al-Nasiri, comandante del sultán mameluco al-Nasir Muhammad ibn y marido de una de sus hijas. Coincidió con el tercer mandato de Qalawun (709-741 / 1309-1340).
keywords: madera tallada; durqa'a; decoración geométrica; arquitectura residencial; arquitectura civil; palacio; mashrabiyya.
partner: Ministry of Culture,Supreme Council of Antiquities

fr.name: Palais de l’émir Bachtak.
description:
Les vestiges de ce palais témoignent encore de sa magnificence et de sa beauté. Ils comprennent la façade ouest, qui donne sur la rue al-Mouiz, et la façade nord, sur Darb (allée) Qurmuz. L'entrée actuelle à arc trilobé se trouve au nord, celle d'origine étant condamnée.  
Certaines parties des premier, deuxième et troisième niveaux ont été préservées. L'architecte a profité de la situation du bâtiment sur l'une des principales artères du Caire médiéval pour aménager des boutiques en rez-de-chaussée. Le hall principal, au second niveau du palais, consiste en une salle centrale (*durqa'a*) entourée d'*iwan*. Elle se distingue par son plafond en bois décoré d'éléments à motifs géométriques d'un travail exquis. Trois degrés de *mouqarnas* en bois ornent les quatre angles du hall. Une fontaine en marbre polychrome, qui rafraîchissait la température, en occupe le centre. Le troisième niveau compte une série de pièces jadis occupées par le harem. Elles donnent sur le hall principal au deuxième niveau par des *aghani*, balcons à arcs brisés fermés par des moucharabiehs en bois tourné percés de petites fenêtres. Les femmes pouvaient ainsi regarder les réceptions pendant lesquelles on chantait et jouait de la musique, qui se tenaient dans le hall mais qui étaient réservées aux hommes.  
Les matériaux de construction utilisés étaient adaptés à l'environnement et au climat chaud de la région du Caire. La pierre, matériau principal, isolait de la chaleur. De même, les sols étaient en marbre, ainsi que certains lambris muraux. Les moucharabiehs protégeaient les femmes du soleil et permettaient une meilleure circulation de l'air dans les appartements.

Les vestiges de ce palais rappellent sa grandeur passée et sa beauté, ainsi qu'il convenait au gendre du sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun. Le palais comprenait les plus beaux éléments de l'architecture civile du Caire : murs de pierre pour isoler du bruit et de la chaleur, plafonds en bois décorés, une fontaine en marbre polychrome, un écran pour offrir une intimité et soulager de la chaleur et de la lumière du soleil, des sols en marbre. Certains aspects de la vie sociale sont identifiables, comme l'affectation de certains espaces réservés aux femmes de la maison et qui donnaient, au travers de jalousies, sur la principale salle de réception des hommes.
artist: Émir Sayf al-Din Bachtak al-Nasiri, l’un des commandants du sultan mamelouk al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun et époux de l’une de ses filles. Il est contemporain du troisième règne d’al-Nasir Muhammad (709-741 H / 1309-1340 J.-C.).
keywords: bois tourné ; durqa’a ; décoration géométrique ; architecture résidentielle ; architecture civile ; palais ; moucharabiehs
partner: Ministry of Culture,Supreme Council of Antiquities

en.name: *The Egyptian University – Faculty of Medicine*
short_description:
General view of the Egyptian University Faculty of Medicine and Qasr al-\`Ayni Hospital in 1933.  
The 1923 Constitution stipulated that “Primary education is mandatory for all Egyptian boys and girls”. A decree was issued for the establishment of a public university under the name “The Egyptian University” in 1925, comprised of four faculties; literature, science, medicine and law. The Faculty of Medicine, annexed to Qasr al-\`Ayni Hospital, is one of the leading hospitals in the Arab World.
keywords: Education; Students; Faculty of Medicine; Egyptian University

en.name: Medallion and Çintamani Ottoman Rug
description:
New styles incorporating chiefly Iranian, but also Mamluk elements, appeared in Turkish Court art as the Ottoman Empire expanded after the capture of Tabriz (1514) and Cairo (1517). The court style developed by the artists, painters, illuminators and calligraphers working in the Court, which started with manuscripts and miniatures, came to dominate every branch of art – jewellery, tiles, fabrics and carpets. The term "court carpets" designates those rugs produced to a very high standard with patterns designed by the court artists. Some of these are products of the court luxury manufactories in Istanbul and others come from workshops supervised by the court (Cairo, Uşak). In the Mamluk carpet weaving manufactory in Cairo, which came under Turkish control in 1517, the hitherto dominant geometric pattern gave way to the court floral style favoured by the Ottomans. It was only the pattern which changed on the Cairene Ottoman carpets; the technical features, asymmetric knots and the use of silk warp and weft threads, stayed the same.  
  
The carpet’s red background is occupied by a central ragged-leaf mandorla with arabesque or *rumi* (arabesque, based on floral, foliate or biomorphic design) lilies framed by *saz* (reed, bullrush) leaves and lotus flowers in the centre. The four corners of the background are cut off by quarter-star medallions of intricate design and *rumi* decorations. The remaining area is occupied by small *çintamani* (Ottoman court motifs of triangular arrangement of three balls above two cloud bands of waves, or a cloud band with one ball) arranged in horizontal rows, offset row by row. The main border is the typical 16th century floral Court style adornment, Chinese lotus flowers and rosettes arranged along an undulating stem, and the outer and inner borders contain alternating red and yellow rosettes strung along an undulating stem. This kind of rug is regarded as a “mass produced” item which the Court workshops made for sale, this evidenced by four known nearly identical rugs (London:Victoria and Albert Museum; Berlin: Museum für Islamische Kunst; Paris: Musée Jacquemart-André; New York: Metropolitan Museum). According to Atıl Esin, four of the five rugs – all except the New York piece – come from the Palazzo Corsi in Florence.
keywords: Cairene-Ottoman Court rug; Çintamani motifs; Silk; Wool
materials: Warp and Weft: silk, pile, wool, asymmetrical (Persian or Senneh) knot
tags: Warp and Weft: silk, pile, wool, asymmetrical (Persian or Senneh) knot

en.name: Sidi Frej Maristan
description:
The Merinid Sultan Abu Yusuf Ya‘qub was responsible, at the end of the 7th/13th century, for the construction of *maristan*s in the town of Fez. There were several of these institutions in Fez, which were intended for the care of mental illness, where each was cared for and provided with medication. But the Sidi Frej *Maristan*, literally “the Lord who delivers”, remains the most famous, continuing to serve, well into the 20th century.  
Frequented by celebrated Andalusian doctors like Abu Bakr al-Qurayshi, who was from Malaga, this hospital was managed by Leon the African, who worked as a agent of the administration of the *maristan* in the 10th/16th century.  
Destroyed in the 20th century, it was replaced by a *funduq* which was, among other things, set aside for trade, and where to this day traditional cosmetic and pharmaceutical products are sold.

es.name: Maristan Sidi Fresh
description:
La construcción de *maristan*es en la ciudad de Fez se remonta al sultán meriní Abu Yusef Ya‘qub, a fines del siglo VII/XIII. Estas instituciones, destinadas a cuidar de los enfermos mentales, eran numerosas; pero el Sidi Fresh —literalmente, “el señor que asiste”— era el más célebre.  
Frecuentado por importantes médicos andalusíes, como el malagueño Abu Bakr al-Korachi, y dirigido por personajes como León el Africano (siglo X/XVI), estuvo en funcionamiento hasta el siglo XX, momento en que fue destruido por un incendio y reemplazado por un *funduq* dedicado especialmente a la venta de productos cosméticos y farmacéuticos tradicionales.

fr.name: Maristan Sidi Frej
description:
La construction de *maristan*s dans la ville de Fès revient au sultan mérinide Abou Youssef Ya‘coub à la fin du VIIe/XIIIe siècle. Ces institutions destinées à soigner les maladies mentales, où chacun trouvait soins et médicaments, étaient nombreuses à Fès. Mais le *maristan* Sidi Frej, littéralement “le Seigneur qui délivre”, reste le plus célèbre et continua à fonctionner jusqu’au XXe siècle.  
Fréquenté par de célèbres médecins andalous comme Abou Bakr al-Korachi, originaire de la ville de Malaga, cet hôpital fut dirigé par Léon l’Africain qui travailla comme agent de l’administration du *maristan* au Xe/XVIe siècle.  
Détruit au XXe siècle, il fut remplacé par un fondouk réservé entre autres aux commerces où se vendent encore aujourd’hui produits cosmétiques et pharmaceutiques traditionnels.

en.name: Çanakkale Rug
description: The rugs of the Çanakkale region are famous for their wool. Pure wool, obtained from sheep owned by the weaver, was used to weave the rugs. All of the steps required for the production of the wool yarn was done within the weavers family. This included shearing the sheep and colouring the fleece with natural dyes. This is a rare and important example of the geometric design typical of Çanakkale rugs. A distinctive pattern of eight arm stars is woven with geometrical border decorations. The field is called a “box” or *sandik* motif. It is a traditional rectangle shape resembling a box containing the bride's trousseau, likely a reference to marriage. The ground of the rug is decorated with flower motifs locally called “apple blossoms”, *elma çiçeği*. The border is decorated with palm tree leaves.
holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
keywords: Çanakkale rug
materials: Natural wool coloured with natural dyes; Gördes knot; symmetrical knot
tags: Natural wool coloured with natural dyes
partner: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts

de.name: Hochaltar
description: Der mächtige Hochaltar mit sechs Säulen über konkavem Grundriss ist im späten 19. Jahrhundert stark verändert worden und konnte bei der 1982 abgeschlossenen Restaurierung in alter Form hergestellt werden. Dabei wurde auch das ursprüngliche Altarblatt wieder eingesetzt, die 1724 von Franz Laukas gemalte Himmelfahrt Mariens. Auch die weiße Fassung der beiden qualitätvollen Standfiguren, der hl. Josef und Joachim, Werke des Bildhauers Andreas Kölle (um 1720), konnte wieder hergestellt werden.

en.name: High altar
description: The imposing high altar with six columns above a concave ground plan was altered considerably in the late 19th century and subsequently returned to its original form during restoration work concluded in 1982. The original altarpiece, the *Assumption of Mary* painted by Franz Laukas in 1724, was also reinserted. The two masterfully executed statues of St. Joseph and Joachim, the work of Andreas Köll (c. 1720) were also repainted white.

en.name: Flag possibly belonging to a group of miners with anarchist ideas, bearing the sign “Neither servants nor masters, nor a penny nor a soldier”

en.name: Miniature
description:
In this miniature, an entire world of living beings—mothers and children, animals, plants, and all forms of life—is depicted within a single drop of water. Beneath the drop appears an Arabic inscription from the Qur’an, Surat al-Anbiya (21:30):  
"*Ve ce‘alnā min al-mā’i kulla shay’in ḥayy*" —  
“We created every living thing from water.”  
  
The work symbolises the idea that all beings are bound together through water, sharing a common origin and interdependence. Reflecting this message, the Istanbul Water Museum has embraced the motto “Su Kardeşliği” — "The Brotherhood of Water."
holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
keywords: Water; Qur'an; Miniature

en.name: *Egypt, Opening of the Suez Canal, Blessing the Canal at Port Said in the Presence of the Imperial and Royal Visitors*
*Apostle Matthew*
description:
The Church and Cloister of the Order of St. Basil in Máriapócs in the Eparchy of Munkács (Mukachevo) was an important centre of the Greek Catholic Church in historical Hungary before the Trianon Peace Treaty of 1920 and the breaking up of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. In this region, the Western Church met with the Eastern churches of the Byzantine ritual, which joined with Rome in 1646. While the 15th and 16th centuries were characterised by the homogeneous Medieval Meta-Byzantine Christian culture of the Eastern churches in the Carpathian region, the 17th century saw modern attitudes surface together with renovation of churches, and the appearance and florescence of a local Late Renaissance style. As the 18th century dawned, a new chapter began in the history of the Eastern churches, one of modernisation, an orientation towards the West and the gradual prevalence of the Baroque.  
Of the iconostases that survive from the second half of the 18th century, the majority were by Galitsian painters, masters from local travelling studios and folk artists. From this time on, Baroque and Rococo features dominated in the style of the icons, as well as the structural elements of the iconostases. Remarkable among these, are works by Mihály (Mihail) and Tádé (Tadeus) Spalinszky. Both originated from Galitzia and became the principal painters of the Eparchy (e.g. the iconostases in Sátoraljaújhely, Ungvár (Uzhorod) and Máriapócs). In 1785, Mihály Spalinszky signed a contract to paint the Máriapócs icons, for which he was paid 130 German Gold coins. The documents relating to the commission are in the Order's archives. This full-figure icon of the Apostle Matthew was isolated from the iconostasis of painted Apostles, all of which were, presumably, after Baroque engravings and painted by the artist Mihály Spalinszky from Galitzia.  
Alongside icons, the Greek Catholic Church and the Eparchy of Munkács (Mukachevo), began to commission new genres such as frescoes, the bishop's portrait gallery and paintings of dignitaries lying in state, all of which became part of the Spalinszky brothers' oeuvre.

en.name: Carpet
description:
The style of this carpet ties it to Mughal court arts; in particular, the red ground floral carpets associated with the palace at Jaipur in northern India. The dark red field is covered with a diaper lattice composed of stylized leaves; inside of each cell is a different spray of flowers. The flowers all grow in the same direction, giving the carpet design a directional orientation; there is only one way to view it so that the flowers are right-side up.  
  
Characteristic of the Mughal floral style is the greater use of botanical details and more complex compositions than in the arts of the neighboring Islamic empires to the West. This is largely because of European herbals, which were major source of inspiration for the Mughal artists. On the other hand, the Mughal artists brought the floral representations to a more idealized state. Mughal flowers are more symmetrically composed and a greater degree of orderliness in the individual details of the plant can be seen compared to their European originals, which arises from naturalistic representations through direct observations.  
  
The way flowers are represented in art depends upon the artist’s medium. Carpet weaving has technical constraints and challenges, and each carpet weaver must confront them by altering and adjusting as they weave. This is especially true for floral designs. It is the pile that carries the designs in carpets. Thus, a carpet design is created knot by knot, row by row. Only a highly skilled weaver can transfer sophisticated curvilinear floral designs such as the ones seen on this carpet to this medium. The materials used for the weaving also need to be very fine so that the weaver can pack as many knots as possible into each square inch to create the curvilinear lines of flowers in a medium which favors 90° angles. In summary, the thickness of yarns used for warp, weft, and pile, the type of knot, the construction of the loom, the skill of the weaver, the complexity of design, and the weaving tradition are all factors that affect the final carpet design.
holder: The George Washington University Museum and The Textile Museum
keywords: Silk; wool; floral motifs; Mughal
materials: Cotton (warp), silk (weft), wool (pile); knotted pile carpet; asymmetrical knot; open left
partner: The George Washington University Museum and The Textile Museum

en.name: Beylerbeyi Palace
short_description: Beylerbeyi Palace was commissioned by Sultan Abdülaziz (1830-76) and built between 1861 and 1865 as a summer residence and a place to entertain visiting heads of state. The Palace was designed by Sarkis Balyan in the second Empire. It looks its most attractive from the Bosporus, from which its two bathing pavilions – one for the *harem* (women's only) and the other for the *selamlik* (men's only) – can best be seen. One of the most attractive rooms is the reception hall, which has a pool and fountain. Running water was popular in Ottoman houses for its pleasant sound and cooling effect in the heat.

en.name: Reliquary of St-George Chiopolites from Aivali
short_description: The reliquary contained the head of George Chiopolites, who was martyred in Aïvali / Kydonies in 1807. The container made for the head has intricate rococo decoration with ribbons, bows, roses, blank heraldic shields and St George holding the attributes of a neomartyr under the imposing two-headed eagle of ecclesiastical authority. From the mid-eighteenth century, thanks to special administrative treatment or privileges, the inhabitants of Aïvali transformed what had been a small fishing village into a flourishing commercial centre on the Aeolian coast. The inscription on the reliquary refers to the goldsmith and to the Guild of Soap-Makers, which was one of the biggest trade associations in the town. It also refers to Sophronios, who oversaw the commissioning, and has been identified to the parish priest and a close relative of Theophilos Kaïris, a teacher at the Academy of Kydonies who was later expelled from the Church under the free Greek state for his revolutionary ideas and was to die in prison, the last ideologue of the Enlightenment.
keywords: relic; rococo

en.name: Bowl with Epigraphic and Vegetal Decoration
description: This strikingly modern bowl is made from humble earthenware, disguised and beautified through the application of a white slip, a semifluid colored clay. Its interior is decorated with an encircling black inscription, and the spaces between the letters are filled by abstract decoration that is augmented by the color red, all covered by a transparent glaze. Read by turning the bowl counterclockwise, the Arabic inscription presents a proverb that retains some resonance even today: “Greed is a sign of poverty.” This proverb, which is inscribed on a number of Samanid bowls, is one of the sayings of the Shi’ite Imam ‘Ali ibn Abu Talib.

en.name: Puppet theatre
description:
During the third quarter of the eighteenth-century the Albicini family from Forlì commissioned this marionette theatre. The coat of arms of the Albicinis' is on the proscenium. The present backdrop and wings show a “magnificent atrium” painted by an artist influenced by the scenography culture of the Bibienas, especially that of Antonio Galli, who was working at that time in Forlì. The backdrop, with its three vanishing points, applies three corner perspective conveying the idea of a space extending behind the visible scene. The theatre has 5 more backdrops and seven pairs of wings, some of which were painted in the nineteenth-century.  
Only some of the marionettes are exhibited; altogether there are 74 male and female figures (some of them are characters from the *Commedia dell'Arte*), 9 horses and 1 monkey. All of the figures were made in the Veneto. The oldest figures are dated to 1750 ca., so they are older than the theatre of which they are part. The others were made in the eighteenth-century. Even if not produced by the same workshop all the marionettes are characterised by similar technical devices including a movable mouth and jointed limbs which moved with a control bar. Some of these marionettes change into something else, a trick widely appreciated at the time (ladies become dwarves and dwarves become giants).  
Puppet theatres were very fashionable in Venice where they were used to represent plays from the *Commedia dell'Arte* and even by comediographer Carlo Goldoni. They were mostly present in noble residences. During the eighteenth-century this habit spread in the north of the country, unfortunately only few survive and we lack information on their use.

This puppet theatre was painted by an artist influenced by the culture of the Bibienas for the Albicini family of Forlì. It is a rare and precious ensemble thanks to the rich equipment of backdrops, wings and marionettes (74 female and male figures, 9 horses and 1 monkey). It was made in Veneto around 1750.

it.name: Teatrino per marionette
description:
Il teatrino per marionette fu commissionato dalla famiglia forlivese Albicini, di cui è dipinto lo stemma sul boccascena, intorno al settimo decennio del Settecento. Nell'attuale allestimento è montato un fondale che raffigura un “atrio magnifico” e due coppie di quinte che completano la scena, dipinte da un artista che ripropone la nuova cultura scenografica dei Bibiena, in particolare di Antonio Galli, attivo proprio in quegli anni a Forlì. Infatti il fondale, con tre fuochi e fuga prospettica centrale, mette in pratica l'accorgimento della visione per angolo e conferisce autonomia allo spazio scenico, suggerendo una ambientazione che continua oltre la scena visibile allo spettatore. Quest'ultimo ha una visione articolata dell'ambientazione da qualsiasi punto di vista stia guardando, anche se non ottimale.  
Oltre ai pezzi esposti al pubblico, il teatrino è dotato di altri 5 fondali e 7 coppie di quinte, alcuni dei quali dipinti nel XIX secolo.  
Anche dell'intero corredo di marionette si può ammirare solo una parte; vi sono 74 figure maschili e femminili (maschere e non), 9 cavalli e 1 scimmia, realizzati in ambito veneto. I pezzi più antichi sono del 1750 ca., quindi precedenti alla costruzione del teatrino assieme al quale ci sono pervenuti; i restanti sono comunque esemplari del XVIII secolo. Pur non essendo state eseguite in una stessa bottega, queste marionette presentano accorgimenti tecnici raffinati e all'avanguardia: bocca mobile, arti snodati e movimentati con il bilanciere. Vi sono anche alcune marionette “a trasformazione”, molto apprezzate all'epoca: dame che si trasformano in nani e nani che diventano giganti.  
I teatrini per marionette erano molto in voga a Venezia per le rappresentazioni delle Commedie dell'arte e dei testi di Goldoni e per lo più erano allestiti nei palazzi della nobiltà. Nel corso del XVIII secolo questo uso si diffuse rapidamente anche nelle altre città del Nord Italia, dove però sono rari i materiali sopravvissuti e le notizie sul loro impiego.

Il teatrino per marionette fu dipinto da un artista di cultura bibienesca nel VII decennio del Settecento per gli Albicini di Forlì. La sua ricca dotazione di fondali, quinte e marionette (74 figure maschili e femminili, 9 cavalli e 1 scimmia realizzati in ambito veneto a partire dal 1750 ca.) ne fa una delle collezioni più importanti del XVIII secolo conservatesi.

en.name: Castle
description:
The palace was built during the reign of Ruggero II (1130-1154), surrounded by the walls of the fortified complex, and was probably used by the Norman court as a cool place to retreat from the summer heat. The earliest information available on this foundation dates from al-Idrisi who, recording Caronia as “*an ancient fortress*” (qal‘a qadima), asserts that near it a new fortalice was built, presuming that the general structure was there before the time of the Normans.  
The complex is delimited by towers and follows the more or less triangular shape of the top of the hill. On both sides of the walls stands a square tower, in an advanced position in relation to the line of the curtain wall. The broad eastern front is made up of two wings of modest outbuildings of a later date. The entry gate erected in 1837 in the style of the Renaissance, hides a pointed doorway standing back, larger, and of an earlier date. The western tower was rebuilt and partly modified in shape following its collapse. At the south-eastern end of the complex there is a third tower, for a long time used as a clock tower.  
The monumental nucleus of the complex consists of the Norman palace of the 12th century, at two levels of analogous structure. On a rectangular plan it has an affinity with the central halls of the palaces of Palermo, Uscibene and Zisa, especially as regards its internal arrangements, with the larger central hall symmetrically flanked by two smaller rooms. The eastern front is characterised by the large entrance portal, which has kept the original frame of double-arched lintels. A particular decorative richness is obtained from the contrasting colours between the golden brown of the large calcareous ashlars and the red colouring of the bricks. The rooms at both levels were originally roofed with vaults, which have only partly been preserved.  
On the upper level, a vault with a lowered roof covers the large central hall. The two rooms flanking the central hall differ considerably from each other. The southern one consists of a rectangular room covered by a low cloister vault with a painted roof, and the central one is a hall consisting of a rectangular room, with a cross vault, open on three sides with large niches (*iwans*), the two lateral ones having fluted umbrella-shaped basons. The niche at the end wall has an elegant device for passing from the rectangular plan to the semi-polygonal one of the bason.  
The chapel, of an uncertain date, stands at the extreme north-east of the complex, and consists of an *aula* divided into three ogival aisles on simple rectangular pillars, ending with semi-circular apses within the thickness of the walls.

es.name: Castillo
description:
Construido durante el reinado de Ruggero II (1130-1154), el palacio, inserto en la muralla del conjunto fortificado, probablemente era utilizado por la corte normanda para aliviarse del calor estival. La noticia más antigua sobre esta construcción nos la proporciona al-Idrisi, quien, recordando Caronia como “peñón antiguo” (*qal‘a qadima*), afirma que cerca de él se había edificado un nuevo fortín, suponemos que refiriéndose a la construcción anterior a la época normanda.  
El conjunto, delimitado por muros con torreones, sigue la geometría de planta más o menos triangular de la cumbre del monte. En ambos lados de la muralla se inserta una torre cuadrada, avanzada respecto a las cortinas. El amplio frente oriental está compuesto por dos alas de modestos anejos, de época posterior. La puerta de entrada, erigida en 1837 con formas renacentistas, esconde un portal rehundido de bóveda de arco apuntado, más antiguo y de mayores dimensiones. La torre occidental se reconstruyó y, en parte, modificó en su forma tras un derrumbamiento. En el extremo sureste del conjunto surge una tercera torre, utilizada durante largo tiempo como torre del reloj.  
El núcleo monumental del conjunto está  
constituido por el palacio normando del siglo XII, de dos pisos con idéntica distribución. De planta rectangular, presenta afinidades con las salas centrales de los palacios palermitanos de Uscibene y la Zisa, sobre todo en la disposición interna, con la sala mayor flanqueada, simétricamente, por dos espacios menores. El frente oriental se caracteriza por la gran puerta de entrada, que conserva el doble marco original en arco. Una particular riqueza decorativa se la da el contraste cromático entre el negro dorado de los gruesos sillares calcáreos y el color rojo de los ladrillos. Los vanos de ambos niveles estaban cubiertos originalmente por bóvedas, que sólo se han conservado en parte. En el piso superior, la gran sala central está cubierta por una bóveda de aljibe rebajada. Las dos estancias que flanquean la sala central difieren notablemente: la meridional está constituida por un vano rectangular cubierto por una bóveda baja de aljibe revocada; la septentrional es una sala formada por un vano rectangular cubierto por una bóveda de crucería, abierto en tres de sus lados por tres grandes nichos (*iwan*s), los dos laterales con bóvedas de cascarón acanaladas. El nicho de la pared del fondo presenta un elegante dispositivo para la transición de la planta rectangular a la semipoligonal del cascarón.  
En el extremo noreste del conjunto fortificado está la capilla, de datación incierta, constituida por una sala de tres naves separadas por arcos ojivales sobre simples pilares rectangulares y que terminan en ábsides semicirculares excavados en el espesor del muro.

en.name: Map of caravan routes
short_description: This map illustrates the trading caravan routes crossing the Sahara desert from Mediterranean ports (Tripoli, Tafilet, Tunis, Algiers and Oran) to sub-Saharan cities. The trading routes were connected north and south to three pilgrim routes for Mecca. The northern pilgrim route from Tunis and Tripoli included Siwah, Cairo, Suez and Aqaba. From Aqaba, meeting the pilgrim route from Damascus, it continued along the coast of Arabia to Mecca. The central route continued from Siwah through the oases of Dakkel and El-Kharjeh to ports on the Red Sea to Jeddah and Mecca. The southern route followed the valley of the Upper Niger through Timbuctu, Gao, Sokoto, Kano, Lake Chad and Kordofan to the port of Swakin on the Red Sea and continued to Jeddah by ship.

en.name: Perfume Bottle
description:
In the middle of the 1st century BC glass-makers along the Syro-Palestinian coast discovered that molten glass could be inflated with air through a hollow blow-pipe. This invention of ‘free-blowing’ revolutionized the glass industry. It allowed vessels to be mass-produced thus rendering them less expensive and available to a wider market so that by the end of the 1st century AD free blown glass vessels were used widely throughout the Roman Empire. The majority were undecorated utilitarian pieces, used for storage and transport, and tablewares, like beakers and plates, but others were embellished with applied decoration. In the free blowing technique, the glass melt, which is taken to the end of the continuous rotating blowing rod, is formed by rolling on the processing table and then blowing. After the internal volume is formed, it is taken to the noble bar from the opposite direction of the blowing rod (usually from the bottom of the container) for operations such as cutting a portion and forming the opening. The forming rod is attached to the container by a drop of the glass melt. Then, in the other direction, the tip of the form is cut or broken to remove the blowing rod. Attachments such as mouth edge profile, base, and handle are also made with auxiliary rods if necessary and then the glass is allowed to cool.  
The type of vessels as seen on this case were used to store liquid perfumes, herbal medicine, liquid seasoning, olive-oil, cider-like fluids and/or as toilet bottles. The technique used to form the thick-walled bottle is the free-blowing technique; blowing striations, bubbles and black impurities are also seen on the surface. The bottle is dark blue-green colour and has a few tool marks at its base. Its rim is folded out, over and in, with bevelled outer lip and flattened into side of mouth. The bottle is in an intact position and has a cylindrical neck and conical body which slightly goes concave to the bottom. On the surfaces, there are some deep weathering and pitting but it also has brilliant iridescence.
keywords: Glass in Asia Minor; Roman period; casting; blowing; mould-blowing

en.name: *Allegorical Tomb of John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough*
description: This painting is part of a series of *Allegorical Tombs* thought of and commissioned by the Irish art dealer Owen McSwiny. It was to be a decoration for the castle of Goodwood which was owned by the dukes of Richmond. The project was intended as a tribute to men who had significantly contributed with their military, political and intellectual capacities to the raise of England after the revolution of 1688. McSwiny chose Venetian and Bolognese artists that specialized in landscapes with architectural ruins. The series was originally conceived of as consisting of 24 paintings, but only some of them, we don't even know how many were completed. This painting was made in collaboration with Donato Creti who painted the figures. Pietro Paltronieri called il Mirandolese was the author of the architecture and Nunzio Ferrajoli painted the landscape. This extremely thorough division of work was the idea of McSwiny and is one of the main features of the series. The elegant and refined figures by Creti convey the historical inspiration and character of a delightful Barocchetto. This is well balanced by the scenery painted by Ferrajoli and Mirandolese. The classical atmosphere helps to soften the sense of morbidity. The tombs, like the ruins of antique monuments are typical of the “capriccio” a very popular genre in the eighteenth-century which aimed to create a pure visual delight for the viewer.

This painting is part of a series of allegorical tombs from the castle Goodwood, owned by the dukes of Richmond.  Donato Creti painted the figures, Nunzio Ferrajoli the landscape and Mirandolese the architectural elements. The depiction of tombs, like that of antique monuments, is a pretext for an elegant visual pleasure, totally free of the theme of death.
keywords: Painting; tomb; allegorical tomb; capriccio; landscape; funerary object; funerary architecture; Arcadia

it.name: Tomba allegorica di John Churchill, duca di Marlborough
description: Il dipinto è parte della serie di “tombe allegoriche” ideate e commissionate dal mercante d’arte irlandese Owen McSwiny per ornare le sale del castello dei duchi di Richmond a Goodwood. Il progetto fu ispirato dalla volontà di conferire un tributo a coloro che avevano contribuito, con imprese militari, politiche e intellettuali, all’ascesa dell’Inghilterra dopo la rivoluzione del 1688. Mac Swiny scelse artisti bolognesi e veneziani, le cui peculiarità artistiche meglio si confacevano alle caratteristiche progettuali orientate verso la tipologia del paesaggio con architetture in rovina. Il progetto doveva comprendere 24 dipinti; ne fu eseguito un numero inferiore, a tutt’oggi non precisabile. L’opera in esame è il risultato della collaborazione tra Donato Creti, autore delle figure, Pietro Paltronieri detto il Mirandolese, per delle architetture, e Nunzio Ferrajoli  per il paesaggio. Questa suddivisione del lavoro secondo forme di estrema specializzazione fu una scelta di McSwiny e costituisce una particolare caratteristica della serie. Le figure eleganti e raffinate di Creti comunicano, nonostante il fine di rimembranza storica del dipinto, i caratteri di un delizioso barocchetto che ben convive con l’ambientazione ideata da Ferrajoli e da Mirandolese  L’atmosfera d’Arcadia che ne deriva allontana il senso della morte del tema tombale e le tombe, come le rovine di monumenti antichi, divengono composizioni tipiche del “capriccio” settecentesco, elementi di un puro diletto sensoriale per l’osservatore.

Il dipinto è parte della serie di “tombe allegoriche” che ornavano il castello dei duchi di Richmond a Goodwood. Donato Creti eseguì le figure, Nunzio Ferrajoli il paesaggio e il Mirandolese le architetture. La raffigurazione delle tombe, come quello delle rovine di monumenti antichi, diviene oggetto di un raffinato diletto sensoriale per l’osservatore, estraneo al tema della morte.
keywords: Dipinto; tomba; tomba allegorica; capriccio; paesaggio; oggetto funerario; architettura funeraria; Arcadia

en.name: Beaker
description: Mamluk beakers are one of the most prolific types of enamelled glass vessels with a wide variety of forms and decorations. This tubular glass beaker has a flared top and a rounded foot. The overall composition of enamelled and polychrome decorations is divided into two main registers outlined by narrow red bands. The first register shows a scene with two figures depicted using thin red lines, each with an enamel, red and blue robe and turban. One of the figures is holding a small beaker while the other sits with his legs crossed. Above them an inscription outlined in red on a blue background reads: “al-malik al-sultan" (The King, the Sultan). These beakers were used as drinking vessels as often depicted in other media from that time.

It mirrors a cartographic plate preserved in a recently discovered manuscript dossier submitted to King Farouk, underscoring efforts to enhance regional connectivity and facilitate pilgrimage.

en.name: *Afshari* carpet
description:
Little is known about the rural rugs of Kirman so authors often describe them as *afshari* only for convenience and not as a precise label. The Afshari appear to be a minority population, although they may be the most important. They are a Turkic tribe with groups in the Caucasus, Turkey and Iran south of Kirman.  
Afshari products are seldom larger than about 170 x 200cm and they tend to be slightly more square-shaped. Some pieces have a striped kilim band at the ends. There are great variations in design, and many motifs found elsewhere are given a fresh approach, such as *boteh*, lozenge-shaped panels, medallion designs with flowers and a stylized vase.  
The central field is divided into nine fields in a form of rhombus. Each field has a horizontal vase motif surrounded with *boteh* and floret motifs. *Boteh* is a universal oriental rug design element. *Boteh* is Persian for “bush” and *buta* is Hindi for “flower”. It is thought to have originated in Kashmir in its curvilinear form. The form and content of botehs are often distinctive for particular areas and may be valuable clues to the origin of a weaving. The central field is framed with four borders. The main border has floral hexagons on narrow sides and on wider sides there is the Y motif between floral hexagons. Two minor borders have zig-zag motifs. On its narrow sides the carpet has kilim finishes.
keywords: Persia; Afshari; Kerman

ar.name: وصفة طبية.
description:
القطعة عبارة عن وصفة طبية مكتوبة على الورق بخط النسخ البسيط المستعمل في الحياة اليومية. و تنسب هذه الوصفة إلى شمس الدين بن العفيف، أحد مشاهير الأطباء في عصر السلطان المملوكي الأشرف برسباي الذي حكم مصر في الفترة من 825 – 841 هـ / 1422 – 1437م. ذكر المؤرخ ابن إياس (المتوفي عام 930 هـ / 1524 م) أن الطبيب شمس الدين بن العفيف كان رئيساً لأطباء مصر ورئيس بيمارستان مصر (بيمارستان السلطان قلاوون)، كما كان الطبيب الخاص للسلطان الأشرف برسباي، وكان أيضاً مسئولاً عن منح الأطباء إذن ممارسة المهنة. ومن الجدير بالذكر هنا، أن المرضى المقيمين في المستشفيات في العصر المملوكي كانوا يلقون رعاية طبية واجتماعية، كما كانت تصرف لهم كسوة. ورواتب إلى أن يتم شفاؤهم. وكان يوقف على البيمارستانات أوقافاً يصرف ريعها على هذه البيمارستانات.  
  
وتصف الوصفة علاج داء الجوف (celiac disease). وهناك بعض الأخطاء اللغوية في كتابة الوصفة التي يمكن قراءة نصها على النحو التالي:  
  
الحمد لله وحده"  
  
سفوف يعرف بسفوف الكفاية من ديوان  
  
ابن العفيف رئيس مرستان مصر قال يؤخذ قرض ربع قدح أنيسون مثله شمار مثله كمون  
  
كرماني وزن أوقيتين … كابلي وفيه سنانير أوقية  
  
بذر كشرت أوقية شيح شامي أوقية لوز أوقيتين  
  
تحمص القرض والشمر ويطحنو ويدق بقية الحوائج  
  
واجمعهم وضف إليهم من ماء الفجل الرملي  
  
ثلاث أواق وماء شمر أخضر مثله وورق حزمتين  
  
ريحان وورق حزمت نعناع وماء عنب ديب  
  
ثلاث أواق ثم ورق حزمت مرسين  
  
طري مدقوق وماء كرفس ثلاث أواق  
  
فيخلط الجميع ويسقي بهم السفوف ثم يجف  
  
ثم يعاد وكذلك حتى يشربو جميع الما(ء)  
  
ويضاف إليهم ربع رطل سكر أبيض  
  
ويسفف منه صباحاً ومساءً نافع  
  
ذلك لداء في الجوف."  
  
وتشير أحدث الدراسات العلمية في علم الغذاء إلى أن بعض أنواع الأغذية قد تسبب أمراضاً تؤدي إلى الوفاة عند بعض المرضى، وأن أحد هذه الأمراض هو داء الجوف. والمصاب بهذا المرض لا يستطيع أن يتعامل مع بروتين القمح نتيجة خلل في وظائف الأمعاء، فإذا تناول القمح أو أحد منتجاته سيعاني من إسهال مزمن ونقص في الوزن يؤدي في النهاية إلى الوفاة. وقد عرف الأطباء في العصر المملوكي هذا المرض. وتصف الوصفة الطبية التي بين أيدينا علاجاً لمرض الجوف الذي توصل إليه العلم الحديث مؤخراً. ويجد المتأمل في مفردات الأعشاب والنباتات التي وردت في هذه الوصفة فوائد عديدة لعلاج أمراض المعدة.

تصف هذه التذكرة الطبية علاجاً لداء يصيب جوف الإنسان، كتبها ابن العفيف، وهو من أشهر أطباء العصر المملوكي، ورئيس بيمارستان قلاوون، الذي كان يعالج فيه أفراد الشعب، مجاناً، دون تمييز، ويصرف لهم الدواء والكسوة والرواتب، مع الرعاية الطبية والإجتماعية، حتى شفائهم.
keywords: حبر؛ خط النسخ؛ دواء؛ طب؛ مرض؛ ورق.

en.name: Medical prescription.
description:
A medical prescription written on paper using a simple *naskhi* script used in daily life. This prescription is attributed to Shams al-Din ibn al-'Afif, one of the most famous physicians practising during the reign of the Mamluk sultan, al-Ashraf Barsbay (r. AH 825–41 / AD 1422–37). The historian Ibn Iyas (d. AH 930 / AD 1524) mentions that al-'Afif was the most eminent doctor in Egypt, and that he was the head of Bimaristan (hospital) of Sultan Qalawun, in Egypt. In addition he was the personal physician to Sultan al-Ashraf Barsbay, and also responsible for granting doctors authorisation to practice. It is important to note here, that the afflicted who resided in Egyptian hospitals during the Mamluk period underwent both social and medical care, for they were clothed and paid until their treatment was finished. There were *Awqaf* (Endowments) made out to these hospitals, the proceeds of which defrayed the costs incurred by these institutions.  
The prescription itself is describing a treatment for the celiac disease. And although there are some grammatical errors in the writing of the description it is readable as follows:  
'*Praise be to the one God* ///  
*A* \[medicinal\] *powder known as “Sufuf al-Kifaya” \[complete in its treatment\] from the diwan of ///*  
*ibn al-'Afif, the head of the maristan of Egypt who said: Take /// a quarter cup of Qaraz \[a pod-like fruit of* Acacia Nilotica\], *the same \[measure\] of aniseed, the same \[measure\] of fennel,/// 2 ounces of Kirmani cumin, … an ounce of mahagony wood, /// an ounce of seed of clover dodder, an ounce of wormwood from al-Sham \[Syria\] and two ounces of almonds./// Roast the qaraz and fennel and grind and crush the remaining components. /// Put hem together and add 3 ounces of water of the sand \[al-ramli\] radish \[to the mixture\] /// and the same measure of the water of green fennel. The leaves /// of two bunches of sweet basil and the leaves of one bunch of mint, 3 ounces of the water of bearberry, /// then the leaves of a fresh chopped-up bunch of sweet myrtle /// and 3 ounces of celery water. /// Mix them together and add to the \[medicinal\] powder, then dry the mixture /// and continue this process until it has soaked up all the water. /// Then add a quarter of a ratl \[a measure, 449.28 g in Egypt today\] of white sugar /// and take it in the morning and evening. This is good /// for the celiac disease.'*  
The latest scientific studies in nutrition indicate that some foods might cause illnesses, which can lead to death. One of these ailments is celiac disease. Those who are afflicted with this disease are not able to absorb wheat protein as a result of a disorder in the function of the intestines. If the sufferer does eat wheat or one of its by-products he or she may develop chronic diarrhoea and weight loss, ending, finally, in death. Doctors during the Mamluk period knew about this illness, and this prescription describes a treatment which modern science arrived at only very recently. Worth contemplating is the variety of herbs and plants that appear on this prescription which have a number of positive effects in the treatment of stomach ailments.

This medical prescription describes a cure for a stomach ailment. It is attributed to Ibn al-‘Afif, the most eminent doctor of the Mamluk period and head of the Bimaristan (hospital) of Sultan Qalawun, where patients were provided with free medicine, clothes and an allowance as well as medical care until their treatment was finished
keywords: Ink; naskhi script; medicine; disease; paper.

es.name: Receta médica.
description:
Receta médica escrita sobre papel en letra *nasji* sencilla, la utilizada en la vida cotidiana. Se atribuye a Shams al-Din ibn al-Afif, uno de los médicos más famosos en época del sultán mameluco al-Ashraf Barsbay (r. 825-841 / 1422-1437). El historiador Ibn Iyas (m. 930 / 1524) dice que era el doctor más eminente de Egipto y responsable del *bimaristan* (hospital) de Qalawun. También era médico personal del sultán y quien concedía a los doctores autorización para ejercer. Es importante destacar que los pacientes de los hospitales egipcios durante el periodo mameluco recibían cuidados médicos pero también sociales, ya que se les proporcionaban ropas y dinero hasta que terminaba su tratamiento. Estos hospitales se sufragaban gracias a donaciones *(waqf)* (donaciones).  
La receta prescribe un tratamiento para la celiaquía. Aunque hay algunos errores gramaticales en el texto, puede leerse lo siguiente:  
“Alabado sea el único Dios / Un polvo \[medicinal\] conocido como “sufuf al-kifaya” del *diwan* de / Ibn al-Afif, responsable del hospital de Egipto, que dijo: Poner / un cuarto de taza de qaraz \[fruto en vainas de la acacia nilótica o espino egipcio\], la misma \[medida\] de anís, la misma de hinojo, / dos onzas de comino kirmani, una onza de madera de caoba,/ una onza de semilla de barbas de capuchino, una onza de ajenjo de al-Sham \[Siria\] y dos onzas de almendras./ Tostar el qaraz y el hinojo y moler y machacar el resto de los ingredientes. / Mezclarlo todo y añadir tres onzas de agua de rábano de la arena / y la misma medida de agua de hinojo fresco. Las hojas / de dos manojos de albahaca dulce y las de un manojo de menta, tres onzas de agua de gayuba; / a continuación, las hojas de un manojo recién picado de arrayán / y tres onzas de agua de apio. / Mezclar y añadir al polvo \[medicinal\] y secar la mezcla después, / y continuar con este proceso hasta que absorba toda el agua. / Añadir un cuarto de *ratl* \[medida equivalente a 449,28 g utilizada en Egipto\] de azúcar blanco / y tomarlo por la mañana y por la noche. Esto es bueno / para la celiaquía.”  
Los últimos estudios científicos sobre nutrición indican que algunos alimentos pueden producir enfermedades, mortales en algunos casos. Una de estas enfermedades es la celiaquía. Quienes la padecen no absorben las proteínas de los cereales debido a una alteración intestinal. Si el enfermo come cereales o alguno de sus derivados, puede sufrir diarrea crónica y pérdidas de peso, e incluso llegar a morir. Los médicos de la época mameluca conocían esta enfermedad y esta receta describe un tratamiento que la ciencia moderna no descubrió hasta hace poco tiempo. Vale la pena fijarse en la variedad de hierbas y plantas que aparecen en la receta y que están indicadas para el tratamiento de las enfermedades gástricas.

Receta médica que describe un tratamiento para una dolencia digestiva. La prescribió Ibn al-Afif, famoso médico de la época mameluca y director del *bimaristan* de Qalawun, donde a los pacientes se les proporcionaban gratuitamente no sólo cuidados y medicamentos, sino también ropa y dinero hasta el fin de su tratamiento.
dates: Siglo IX de la Hégira / XV d. C.
keywords: Tinta; escritura nasji medicina; enfermedad; papel

fr.name: Ordonnance médicale.
description:
Ordonnance médicale rédigée sur papier en écriture *naskhi* courante. Elle est attribuée à Chams al-Din ibn al-Afif, l'un des plus célèbres médecins du règne du sultan mamelouk al-Achraf Barsbay (r. 825-841 H / 1422-1437 J.-C.). L'historien Ibn Ilyas (mort en 930 H / 1524 J.-C.) affirme qu'il était le plus éminent praticien d'égypte. Médecin personnel du sultan Barsbay, il dirigeait l'hôpital (*bimaristan*) du sultan Qalawun et avait le pouvoir d'autoriser les nouveaux praticiens à exercer. Les malades qui séjournaient dans les hôpitaux égyptiens pendant la période mamelouke bénéficiaient d'un traitement à la fois médical et social puisqu'ils étaient vêtus et rémunérés jusqu'à la fin de leur traitement. Des *awqaf* (fondations) finançaient ces hôpitaux.  
L'ordonnance porte sur un traitement pour la maladie cœliaque. Bien qu'elle comporte quelques erreurs grammaticales, elle se lit comme suit :  
“Louange au seul Dieu… / Une poudre \[médicinale\] appelée “Soufouf al-Kifaya” du *diwan* de / Ibn al-'Afif, responsable du *maristan* d'égypte, qui dit : Prendre / un quart de coupe de *qaraz* \[fruit en gousse de l'*Acacia nilotica*\], la même \[mesure\] de semence d'anis, la même de fenouil, / deux onces de cumin Kirmani, … une once de bois d'acajou, / une once de semence de clou de cuscute, une once d'armoise de al-Cham \[Syrie\] et deux onces d'amandes. / Faire rôtir le *qaraz* et le fenouil puis moudre et broyer les restes. / Mélangez-les et ajoutez 3 onces de décoction de radis de sable \[*al-ramli*\] / et la même quantité de décoction de fenouil vert. Les feuilles / de deux bouquets de basilic doux et les feuilles d'un bouquet de menthe, 3 onces de décoction de cerise d'ours, / puis les feuilles d'un bouquet de myrte douce fraîchement coupée / et 3 onces de décoction de céleri. / Mélanger le tout ensemble et ajouter à la poudre médicinale, puis sécher le mélange / et continuez jusqu'à ce qu'il ait exprimé toute son eau. / Puis ajouter un quart de *ratl* \[mesure correspondant à 449,28 g\] de sucre blanc / et prenez le matin et le soir. C'est bon / pour la maladie cœliaque.  
Les plus récentes études scientifiques de nutrition indiquent que certains aliments peuvent provoquer des maladies, et même la mort. L'une de ces affections est la maladie cœliaque, dont les victimes ne peuvent consommer de protéines de blé par suite d'un désordre intestinal. Elle peut provoquer des diarrhées, des pertes de poids et finalement la mort. Au cours de la période mamelouke, les médecins connaissaient cette affection et cette ordonnance décrit un traitement auquel la science moderne n'est arrivée que récemment. Les diverses herbes et plantes citées exercent un certain nombre d'effets sur les traitements des maux d'estomac.

Cette ordonnance médicale détaille un traitement pour un mal à l'estomac. On l'attribue à Ibn al-Afif, le docteur le plus éminent de la période mamelouke et chef du *bimaristan* (hôpital) du sultan Qalawun, où les patients recevaient gratuitement médicaments et vêtements, et bénéficiaient de subsides et de soins médicaux jusqu'à la fin de leur traitement.
dates: IXe siècle de l’Hégire (XVe siècle J.-C.).
keywords: encres ; écriture naskhi ; médecine ; maladies ; papier
